progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From B5a: mitosis gives two identical daughter cells, and a body grows from one zygote by mitosis. From B5b: meiosis makes gametes; fertilisation makes a zygote. From B6b: a gene is a stretch of DNA coding for a polypeptide; RNA polymerase binds the promoter before copying the gene into mRNA. From B6c: codons are translated into amino acids. From B9: a heterozygous parent passes an allele to each child with a one in two chance. From bg03 (Module 5, G03): a BRCA variant raises cancer risk without guaranteeing cancer. From b01: a mutation makes a new allele; in animals a mutation is passed on only if it is in a cell that makes eggs or sperm, and a skin-cell mutation affects only that animal. From b02: UV damages skin cells. From b03: silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift. From b04: chromosomal mutations, including the somatic leukaemia swap. Not assumed: somatic and germ-line as named mutation types with their effects, coding and non-coding DNA, regulatory sequence, intron, lactase persistence.
progression.startsWith: Place the same mutation in a body cell or a germ-line cell, and in a coding or non-coding stretch. The video opens: In 2013, Angelina Jolie said she carried a mutation in a gene called B R C A one.
progression.stopsAfter: distinguishing somatic mutations (in body cells; copied by mitosis into a patch of descendant cells, larger if earlier; can affect that organism, including by starting a cancer; not inherited in animals) from germ-line mutations (in cells that make gametes; present in every cell of an offspring that inherits it, including its germ cells, so it can be passed on and enter the gene pool, while the parent in which it arose is unaffected); stating that only about 1 to 2 per cent of human DNA codes for protein; explaining that a coding mutation changes a codon (silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift) while a mutation in a promoter or regulatory sequence changes how much, when or where a gene is expressed with every codon unchanged (lactase persistence); explaining that a change in an intron usually has no effect unless it hits the cut signal, and that some non-coding DNA has no known job; assessing coding against non-coding significance by what the changed stretch does, not by whether it is translated; combining both questions in a two-by-two grid; applying this to an unseen fruit fly distinguish item and an unseen promoter against silent substitution assess item.
progression.nextLesson: practise mutation effects on exam-style questions (route entry bio-m6-g01), then how meiosis and fertilisation vary offspring (bio-m6-b07).

teaching.task: A mutation's effect depends on where it happens, so where in the body and where in the DNA, and what difference does each make?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why a somatic mutation stays in a patch (mitosis copies it only into the mutated cell's descendants, 3); why timing changes the patch (an earlier cell has more descendants, 3); why a patch can become a cancer (more mutations in division-control genes, 3); why a germ-line mutation reaches every cell of the offspring (it is in the zygote, 4) and can go on (it reaches the offspring's germ cells, 4); why the parent is unaffected (only its germ line carries it, 4); why a promoter change matters with every codon correct (the polymerase binds less well, less mRNA, 7); why lactase persistence keeps lactase (the switch stays on, 8); why most intron changes do nothing but a cut-signal change can (introns are removed; the cut signal decides what is kept, 9); why neither coding nor non-coding wins as a rule (significance follows what the stretch does, 10). Visible case: one tree of cells carries every somatic and germ-line idea; one gene map carries every coding and non-coding idea; one grid joins them. Video advantage: the patch grows as cells divide, a whole tree lights from one zygote, the polymerase slips and the amount bar falls, the intron lifts out. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; the attempt 2 card is the densest frame and is the task itself.
teaching.conversationalApproach: The same BRCA1 change, inherited in every cell or arising later in one breast cell, sets two questions: where in the body, and where in the DNA; the cell lineage tree shows somatic and germ-line cells before they are named, then a somatic mutation filling only one patch (larger if earlier, sometimes a cancer) and a germ-line mutation reaching every cell and the next generation; the distinction answers the hook; the gene map then shows coding DNA, control stretches (promoter, regulatory sequences) and lactase persistence as a real regulatory change that spread in milk-drinking populations; introns and DNA with no known job are placed; coding against non-coding is a judgement, not a rule; a two-by-two grid joins both questions. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback, then the decision rule hands off to the mutation practice video (g01).
teaching.openingDecision: In 2013, Angelina Jolie said she carried a mutation in a gene called B R C A one. She'd inherited it, so it was in every cell of her body, and her doctors estimated her breast cancer risk at eighty-seven per cent. But the same change can also happen later in life, in a single breast cell, and then no child can inherit it. So why does it matter which cell a mutation is in, and which part of the DNA?
teaching.understandingCheck: 13a is a distinguish item on fruit flies exposed to X-rays as larvae: fly A has a mutation in one developing eye cell and grows up with a small patch of white facets in one red eye; fly B has a mutation in a cell that makes sperm and looks normal. (a) Identify each as somatic or germ-line; (b) explain how their effects differ on the fly itself and on its offspring. It tests both halves of the B6-IQ1-03 verb (scenes 3 to 5). 13c is an assess item: two substitutions in one enzyme gene, P in the promoter (cells make about a tenth as much mRNA) and Q in the coding sequence (codon CUU to CUC, chart excerpt given), against a student's claim that Q matters more because it is coding. It tests B6-IQ1-04's verb: a judgement with a reason for each segment type. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 s): answer, key reason, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B6-IQ1-03: "distinguish between somatic mutations and germ-line mutations and their effect on an organism   (ACSBL082, ACSBL083)". B6-IQ1-04: "assess the significance of ‘coding’ and ‘non-coding’ DNA segments in the process of mutation (ACSBL078)". The three spaces before "(ACSBL082" and the curly quotes around ‘coding’ and ‘non-coding’ are in the official DOCX extraction and are kept verbatim in the YouTube block. This video owns first coverage of both rows; update the ledger rows for B6-IQ1-03 and B6-IQ1-04 when this design passes review. The two verbs are carried by the attempts: "distinguish ... and their effect on an organism" (attempt 1, both halves) and "assess" (attempt 2, a judgement with reasons).

design.visualSystem: Two boards, then one grid that joins them. (1) The cell lineage board (scenes 1 to 5): a coded `CellTree`, one cream zygote circle at the top dividing downward into rows of small cell circles (1, 2, 4, 8, then a dense fan of about 60), drawn in thin ink like a family tree; a mutation is an amber dot inside a cell, and every cell descended from it fills with a pale amber tint as the tree grows. A small side branch is tinted plum and labelled once, "germ line" (the cells that make eggs or sperm); the rest is cream, "body (somatic)". Real objects are painted and sit beside the tree, never inside it: `m6-uv-skin-v1.png` and `m8-skin-melanoma-v1.png` (skin), `m6-egg-sperm-dish-v1.png` and `b3a-sperm-v1.png` (gametes). No people: the hook names a person but shows only a chromosome pair and cells. (2) The gene map (scenes 6 to 10): one long b01 `SlimStrand` across the board with regions as soft bands: a far control stretch (teal, small), the promoter (teal), the gene's coding stretches (warm bands) separated, from scene 9, by introns (thin grey loops lifted slightly above the strand), and long plain grey stretches either side. A coded RNA polymerase blob (B6b's look) sits on the promoter; an mRNA row (typeset terracotta text, codons spaced, as in b03) and a coded protein blob with a small amount bar sit above. A mutation is one amber rung with b01's `BaseSwap` callout. Codons are typeset text, never tiles; the strand stays slim. (3) The grid (scene 11): two by two, columns "somatic" and "germ line", rows "coding" and "non-coding", each cell holding one small icon and two to five words. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items on screen at once besides small grey region labels; each tag fades when the next cue lands; the tree's "germ line" and "body" labels fade after scene 2 and return only in scene 5.
design.transitionPlan: The hook's chromosome pair and two cell trees open the cell lineage board; the trees grow, tint and return small for the distinction; the card clears to the gene map, where bands, the polymerase blob, the mRNA row and the protein bar change on each cue and introns lift above the strand; the lactase plate sits beside the map; the map dims and shrinks for the judgement and gives way to the two-by-two grid; memory lines write on large; each attempt clears the board and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the model answer one point at a time; the step chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
